Credit Risk Scoring & Default Prediction¶

A consumer-credit default model, calibrated risk scoring, and regulator-style adverse action explanations¶

Goal. Predict the probability that a consumer-credit applicant will default, turn that probability into an interpretable credit score / risk band, and — going one step beyond a typical scoring notebook — automatically generate ECOA/Reg B–style "adverse action" reason codes for declined applicants, the way a real lender is legally required to.

Dataset. A classic consumer credit-scoring dataset (4,455 loan applicants, gastonstat/CreditScoring, based on a data-mining course dataset widely used in credit-risk teaching material). Each row is one loan application with applicant financials (income, assets, debt, employment tenure, etc.) and the outcome (good / bad repayment).

2. Exploratory data analysis¶

First, the target. Consumer-credit portfolios are usually imbalanced — most applicants repay — and this one is no exception, so accuracy alone would be a misleading metric (predicting "everyone is good" gets ~72% accuracy for free). That's exactly why the brief calls for ROC-AUC / PR-AUC instead.

3. Missing value treatment¶

This dataset encodes missing data two different ways, which is worth catching before it silently corrupts a model:

  • Numeric sentinel: income, assets, debt use 99999999 to mean "not reported". Left as-is, a model would read that as an implausibly high income — exactly backwards.
  • Categorical sentinel: home, marital, job use 0 to mean "unknown".

Treatment: convert both sentinels to real NaN, add missingness indicator flags for the numeric fields (whether income was missing can itself be predictive — e.g. self-employed applicants under-report income), then median/mode-impute inside the modelling pipeline (fit on train only).

In [7]:
SENTINEL = 99999999
num_sentinel_cols = ["income", "assets", "debt"]
cat_unknown_cols = ["home", "marital", "job"]

df = df[df["status"] != 0].copy()                       # drop the single unlabeled row
df["default"] = (df["status"] == 2).astype(int)         # 1 = bad/default, 0 = good
df.drop(columns=["status"], inplace=True)

missing_report = {}
for c in num_sentinel_cols:
    missing_report[c] = int((df[c] == SENTINEL).sum())
    df[c] = df[c].replace(SENTINEL, np.nan)
for c in cat_unknown_cols:
    missing_report[c] = int((df[c] == 0).sum())
    df[c] = df[c].replace(0, np.nan)

print("Missing values found per column:")
for k, v in missing_report.items():
    print(f"  {k:10s}: {v}")

for c in num_sentinel_cols:
    df[c + "_was_missing"] = df[c].isna().astype(int)

4. Feature engineering¶

records is recoded to a clean 0/1 flag. Four ratio features are added — these are standard credit-underwriting signals (debt-to-income, loan-to-income, installment burden, and financed % of purchase price) and, as the SHAP section later shows, they turn out to matter more than most of the raw fields on their own.

In [8]:
df["records"] = df["records"].map({1: 0, 2: 1})   # 1 = has derogatory record
eps = 1.0
df["debt_to_income"]        = df["debt"]   / (df["income"] + eps)
df["loan_to_income"]        = df["amount"] / (df["income"] + eps)
df["installment"]           = df["amount"] / df["time"].replace(0, np.nan)
df["installment_to_income"] = df["installment"] / (df["income"] + eps)
df["finance_ratio"]         = df["amount"] / df["price"].replace(0, np.nan)   # % of price financed

target = "default"
num_features  = ["seniority", "time", "age", "expenses", "income", "assets", "debt",
                  "amount", "price", "debt_to_income", "loan_to_income",
                  "installment_to_income", "finance_ratio"]
cat_features  = ["home", "marital", "job"]
bin_features  = ["records", "income_was_missing", "assets_was_missing", "debt_was_missing"]
RATIO_COLS    = ["debt_to_income", "loan_to_income", "installment_to_income"]

X = df[num_features + cat_features + bin_features].copy()
y = df[target].copy()
print(X.shape, "| default rate:", round(y.mean(), 3))

(4454, 20) | default rate: 0.282

5. Train / test split & preprocessing¶

A 75/25 stratified split keeps the ~28% default rate consistent in both sets. The three engineered ratio features get winsorized at the 99th percentile — a handful of near-zero-income applicants otherwise produce absurd ratios (debt-to-income in the thousands) that would dominate a linear model. Caps are learned on the training set only and applied to test, to avoid leakage.

In [9]:
X_train, X_test, y_train, y_test = train_test_split(
    X, y, test_size=0.25, stratify=y, random_state=RANDOM_STATE
)

for c in RATIO_COLS:
    cap = X_train[c].quantile(0.99)
    X_train[c] = X_train[c].clip(upper=cap)
    X_test[c]  = X_test[c].clip(upper=cap)

print("Train:", X_train.shape, " Test:", X_test.shape)

Train: (3340, 20)  Test: (1114, 20)

6. Baseline model — Logistic Regression¶

The interpretable baseline. Numeric features are median-imputed and scaled; categoricals are one-hot encoded. class_weight="balanced" compensates for the ~28% default rate instead of letting the model default to predicting "good" for everyone.

In [10]:
numeric_transform = Pipeline([
    ("impute", SimpleImputer(strategy="median")),
    ("scale", StandardScaler()),
])
cat_transform_ohe = Pipeline([
    ("impute", SimpleImputer(strategy="most_frequent")),
    ("ohe", OneHotEncoder(handle_unknown="ignore")),
])
preprocess_logit = ColumnTransformer([
    ("num", numeric_transform, num_features),
    ("cat", cat_transform_ohe, cat_features),
    ("bin", "passthrough", bin_features),
])

logit_pipe = Pipeline([
    ("prep", preprocess_logit),
    ("clf", LogisticRegression(max_iter=2000, class_weight="balanced", random_state=RANDOM_STATE)),
])
logit_pipe.fit(X_train, y_train)
logit_proba = logit_pipe.predict_proba(X_test)[:, 1]

print(f"Logistic Regression  ROC-AUC: {roc_auc_score(y_test, logit_proba):.4f}"
      f"   PR-AUC: {average_precision_score(y_test, logit_proba):.4f}")

Logistic Regression  ROC-AUC: 0.8455   PR-AUC: 0.7035
In [11]:
# interpretability: which features push risk up / down?
ohe_names = logit_pipe.named_steps["prep"].named_transformers_["cat"].named_steps["ohe"].get_feature_names_out(cat_features)
all_names = num_features + list(ohe_names) + bin_features
coefs = pd.Series(logit_pipe.named_steps["clf"].coef_[0], index=all_names).sort_values()

fig, ax = plt.subplots(figsize=(7, 7))
pd.concat([coefs.head(8), coefs.tail(8)]).plot(kind="barh", ax=ax, color="#4C72B0")
ax.set_title("Logistic Regression coefficients (positive = higher default risk)")
ax.axvline(0, color="black", linewidth=0.8)
plt.tight_layout()
plt.show()

7. XGBoost¶

A gradient-boosted tree model to capture non-linearities and interactions the logistic baseline can't (e.g. the effect of debt-to-income may depend on employment tenure). scale_pos_weight handles the class imbalance the way class_weight="balanced" did for logistic regression.

In [12]:
xgb_prep = ColumnTransformer([
    ("num", SimpleImputer(strategy="median"), num_features),
    ("cat", SimpleImputer(strategy="most_frequent"), cat_features),
    ("bin", "passthrough", bin_features),
])
Xtr_xgb = xgb_prep.fit_transform(X_train, y_train)
Xte_xgb = xgb_prep.transform(X_test)
feat_names_xgb = num_features + cat_features + bin_features

scale_pos_weight = (y_train == 0).sum() / (y_train == 1).sum()
xgb_clf = xgb.XGBClassifier(
    n_estimators=300, max_depth=4, learning_rate=0.05,
    subsample=0.9, colsample_bytree=0.9, reg_lambda=1.0,
    scale_pos_weight=scale_pos_weight, eval_metric="auc",
    random_state=RANDOM_STATE, n_jobs=-1,
)
xgb_clf.fit(Xtr_xgb, y_train)
xgb_proba = xgb_clf.predict_proba(Xte_xgb)[:, 1]

print(f"XGBoost               ROC-AUC: {roc_auc_score(y_test, xgb_proba):.4f}"
      f"   PR-AUC: {average_precision_score(y_test, xgb_proba):.4f}")

XGBoost               ROC-AUC: 0.8450   PR-AUC: 0.6962

8. Model evaluation¶

ROC-AUC and PR-AUC side by side, plus a confusion matrix at a chosen operating threshold. PR-AUC matters more here than in a balanced problem — it's much more sensitive to how well the model finds the minority "bad" class, which is what actually drives lending losses.

In [13]:
results = pd.DataFrame({
    "model": ["Logistic Regression", "XGBoost"],
    "roc_auc": [roc_auc_score(y_test, logit_proba), roc_auc_score(y_test, xgb_proba)],
    "pr_auc":  [average_precision_score(y_test, logit_proba), average_precision_score(y_test, xgb_proba)],
})
results

9. Probability calibration¶

Raw XGBoost probabilities are typically not well calibrated — a "0.7" from the model doesn't necessarily mean a true 70% default rate, which matters a lot here because the whole point of the next section is to translate probabilities directly into a score. Isotonic calibration (5-fold, out-of-fold) is used and validated with the Brier score — the standard metric for how well predicted probabilities match observed outcomes (lower is better) — and a reliability curve.

In [16]:
print(f"Brier score, uncalibrated XGBoost: {brier_score_loss(y_test, xgb_proba):.4f}")

xgb_for_calib = xgb.XGBClassifier(
    n_estimators=300, max_depth=4, learning_rate=0.05,
    subsample=0.9, colsample_bytree=0.9, reg_lambda=1.0,
    scale_pos_weight=scale_pos_weight, eval_metric="auc",
    random_state=RANDOM_STATE, n_jobs=-1,
)
calib = CalibratedClassifierCV(xgb_for_calib, method="isotonic", cv=5)
calib.fit(Xtr_xgb, y_train)
calib_proba = calib.predict_proba(Xte_xgb)[:, 1]

print(f"Brier score, calibrated XGBoost:   {brier_score_loss(y_test, calib_proba):.4f}")
print(f"ROC-AUC is rank-based so it barely moves with calibration: {roc_auc_score(y_test, calib_proba):.4f}")

Brier score, uncalibrated XGBoost: 0.1518

Brier score, calibrated XGBoost:   0.1372
ROC-AUC is rank-based so it barely moves with calibration: 0.8438
In [17]:
fig, ax = plt.subplots()
for proba, label in [(xgb_proba, "uncalibrated"), (calib_proba, "isotonic-calibrated")]:
    frac_pos, mean_pred = calibration_curve(y_test, proba, n_bins=10, strategy="quantile")
    ax.plot(mean_pred, frac_pos, marker="o", label=label)
ax.plot([0, 1], [0, 1], "k--", linewidth=0.8, label="perfectly calibrated")
ax.set_xlabel("Mean predicted probability"); ax.set_ylabel("Observed default rate"); ax.set_title("Reliability curve")
ax.legend()
plt.show()

Global feature importance from SHAP values on the (uncalibrated-structure) XGBoost model. This isn't just for the plot below — the same per-applicant SHAP values power the adverse-action reason codes in Section 12.

explainer = shap.TreeExplainer(xgb_clf)
sv = explainer(pd.DataFrame(Xte_xgb, columns=feat_names_xgb))

shap.plots.beeswarm(sv, max_display=12, show=False)

The engineered ratio features (finance_ratio, loan_to_income, debt_to_income) rank among the most important — a nice sanity check that the feature engineering in Section 4 earned its keep.

11. Credit score & risk-band framework¶

Calibrated probabilities are converted to a familiar 3-digit score using the same log-odds (PDO) formula real bureaus use:

$$\text{score} = \text{offset} + \text{factor} \times \ln(\text{odds of good})$$

Design choice: the formula is anchored to this portfolio's own average odds (≈28% default rate) rather than borrowing a generic prime-book constant like "50:1 good:bad at 600" — that constant assumes a much safer population than this one and would push almost everyone into the bottom band, which is a common mistake in tutorial versions of this technique.

Risk bands are then cut by score quantile (5 equal-sized groups) and validated against the actual observed default rate in each group — a set of bands is only useful if real-world risk actually increases monotonically band to band.

In [20]:
avg_bad_rate = y_train.mean()
base_odds = (1 - avg_bad_rate) / avg_bad_rate
BASE_SCORE, PDO = 650, 50
factor = PDO / np.log(2)
offset = BASE_SCORE - factor * np.log(base_odds)

p_bad = np.clip(calib_proba, 1e-6, 1 - 1e-6)
odds_good = (1 - p_bad) / p_bad
score = offset + factor * np.log(odds_good)
score = np.clip(score, 300, 850)   # cosmetic clip to a familiar 300-850 scale

score_series = pd.Series(score, index=y_test.index, name="credit_score")
score_series.describe()

12. Extension — Adverse Action Reason Codes (regulatory-style explainability)¶

Why this matters. In the US, the Equal Credit Opportunity Act (ECOA) and Regulation B require lenders who deny credit to give applicants specific, principal reasons for the denial — not just "declined." In practice this is usually implemented as the top 2–4 factors that most hurt the applicant's score, sourced from the underwriting model. Most portfolio credit-scoring projects stop at a global SHAP importance plot; this section turns those same SHAP values into per-applicant, compliance-styled reason codes, which is closer to what a real credit-risk or MLE team actually has to ship.

A deliberate design decision: the model itself can see age, marital, and home (residential type), and they do carry predictive signal — but they are excluded from the customer-facing reason-code vocabulary below. Marital status is an explicitly protected class under ECOA; age is tightly regulated; residential type can proxy geography and, historically, protected characteristics (redlining). A reason code is a compliance artifact, not just a model explanation, so it's restricted to defensible ability-to-repay factors only.

In [23]:
ALLOWED_REASON_FEATURES = {
    "seniority":              "Limited length of employment / job tenure",
    "income":                 "Insufficient income relative to obligations",
    "assets":                 "Limited asset reserves / collateral",
    "debt":                   "High level of existing debt",
    "debt_to_income":         "High ratio of total debt to income",
    "loan_to_income":         "Requested loan amount high relative to income",
    "installment_to_income":  "Monthly installment high relative to income",
    "finance_ratio":          "High proportion of purchase price being financed",
    "records":                "History of delinquent credit obligations",
    "expenses":               "High level of recurring expenses",
    "amount":                 "Requested loan amount",
    "time":                   "Requested repayment term",
    "job":                    "Employment category / stability",
}

EXCLUDED_NOTE = (
    "Excluded from customer-facing reasons (kept in the model, never shown as a 'reason for denial'): "
    "age, marital, home, and the internal *_was_missing flags."
)
print(EXCLUDED_NOTE)

def adverse_action_reasons(row_shap, feature_names, top_n=4):
    """Top-N allowed factors pushing THIS applicant's predicted risk up, as ECOA-style reason strings."""
    pairs = [(f, v) for f, v in zip(feature_names, row_shap) if f in ALLOWED_REASON_FEATURES]
    pairs.sort(key=lambda x: x[1], reverse=True)          # positive SHAP -> pushes toward default
    return [ALLOWED_REASON_FEATURES[f] for f, v in pairs[:top_n] if v > 0]

Excluded from customer-facing reasons (kept in the model, never shown as a 'reason for denial'): age, marital, home, and the internal *_was_missing flags.
In [24]:
# apply the score/band decision to every test applicant, then generate reason codes for every DECLINE
decision_df = pd.DataFrame({
    "credit_score": score_series.values,
    "band": bands.values,
    "true_default": y_test.values,
}, index=y_test.index)

declined_mask = decision_df["band"].isin(["E - Decline", "D - High Risk"]).values
declined_positions = np.where(declined_mask)[0]
print(f"{declined_mask.sum()} of {len(decision_df)} test applicants fall in a decline-tier band.")

reason_lists = [None] * len(decision_df)
for pos in declined_positions:
    reason_lists[pos] = adverse_action_reasons(sv.values[pos], feat_names_xgb, top_n=4)
decision_df["adverse_action_reasons"] = reason_lists

# portfolio-level view: which reasons show up most often across ALL declines?
from collections import Counter
reason_counter = Counter()
for r_list in decision_df.loc[declined_mask, "adverse_action_reasons"]:
    reason_counter.update(r_list)

reason_freq = pd.Series(reason_counter).sort_values(ascending=True)
fig, ax = plt.subplots(figsize=(8, 5))
reason_freq.plot(kind="barh", ax=ax, color="#8172B2")
ax.set_title("Most common adverse-action reasons across all declined test applicants")
ax.set_xlabel("Number of applicants citing this reason (top-4 each)")
plt.tight_layout()
plt.show()

This is the kind of output a fair-lending / compliance reviewer would actually want to see: not just "the model is 84% accurate," but a defensible, per-applicant, auditable reason for every automated decline — sourced directly from the same SHAP values already used for model interpretability.

13. Conclusion & next steps¶

What this project shows:

  • A full pipeline from raw applicant data → calibrated default probability → business-usable credit score & risk bands, evaluated on ROC-AUC / PR-AUC rather than accuracy given the class imbalance.
  • Two models (interpretable logistic baseline vs. XGBoost), both calibrated and validated with a reliability curve and Brier score.
  • Risk bands that are validated, not just asserted — observed default rate increases monotonically from Prime to Decline.
  • An extension most portfolio projects skip: regulator-style adverse action reason codes, generated per-applicant from SHAP values, with an explicit, documented exclusion list for legally sensitive features.

If this went to production, the next steps would be:

  • Reject inference — the model is only trained on applicants who were actually funded; true population default rates for rejected applicants are unobserved and would bias the score over time.
  • Fair-lending / disparate-impact testing — even with protected features excluded from reason codes, the underlying model's decisions should be tested for disparate impact across protected groups before deployment.
  • Population Stability Index (PSI) monitoring — track whether the incoming applicant population is drifting away from the population the model was trained on.
  • Champion/challenger threshold tuning — pick the score cutoff using the lender's actual cost of a missed default vs. cost of a lost good customer, not a fixed 0.5 threshold.
